newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Sunday weekend seen boosting Pakistani exports.
newsitem.headline: Sunday weekend seen boosting Pakistani exports.

text.p: Islamic Pakistan, aligning itself with the global marketplace, has reverted to a Sunday weekend for the first time in two decades.
Bankers and businessmen welcomed the move, one of the first actions of newly- elected Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, saying it would make it easier to trade with the outside world.
Conservative Islamic clerics opposed the change, but Sharif's huge parliamentary majority meant he did not need the support of religious parties as his predecessor Benazir Bhutto did.
Bhutto's father, then prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, introduced the Friday weekend in 1977 to appease the clergy, who saw the Sunday holiday as a legacy of British rule.
"We still consider the Friday weekend as good for Moslems," Ghafoor Ahmed, deputy chief of the religious Jamaat-i-Islami party, which denounced Sharif's move, said on Friday.
Businessmen now expect better links with the outside world, where Friday is a working day for all but Islamic countries.

"The working week in Pakistan now coincides with the international working week," said a member of the Overseas Investors Chamber of Commerce and Industry, who asked not to be named. "Such a move would have a number of benefits."

It would bring Pakistan in line with its main trading rivals and enable it to do business with the rest of the world for five instead of four days a week, he said. It would also send a strong signal to international investors that Pakistan is keen to be taken seriously as an arena for investment.

"Pakistan was effectively cut off from the United States for three-and-a-half days and from Europe for three days due to the Friday weekly holiday," an official of the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry said.
Commodity traders said the change would help their business.
"Our cotton yarn exports are expected to rise sharply due to the change in weekend," said Hasnain Ahmed, secretary of the Pakistan Yarn Merchants Association.

Sales of cotton yarn, Pakistan's top export, brought in $801 million in the first seven months of fiscal 1996/97 (July-June), followed by cotton fabrics at $672 million and readymade garments at $416 million.
"We will boost our rice exports," said Javed Islam Agha, chairman of the Rice Exporters Association of Pakistan. Rice exports totalled $237 million in the first seven months.

"The decision will accelerate exports and augment foreign exchange earnings as Pakistani exporters will remain in contact with the international market for five days a week," said Maqbool Sadiq, head of the private Karachi Cotton Association.
Stock brokers said it would help foreign investors. "We expect more buying of Pakistani stocks by overseas investors on Fridays," said Arif Habib, head of the Karachi Stock Exchange.
The bourse, along with some industrialists, attempted a unilateral reversion to a Sunday weekend in October, but had to drop the plan in the teeth of protests from religious groups.

Educators welcomed the Sunday weekend. "It will have good psychological and social implications on students, who are likely to get more hours to study," said Anita Ghulam Ali, a former education minister in the Sindh provincial government.
Sharif ordered the change in a televised address a week ago, six days after taking office following his Pakistan Muslim League party's landslide victory in February 3 elections.
